title: From Tiny to Towering
objectives: I can use ten words to tell exactly how big, small, or roomy something is.
I can put size words in order from smallest to biggest.
I can use a picture and context clues to choose the best size word.
I can write a description that uses exact size words instead of big and small.
rationale: Size is the easiest scale to picture, so it is the first shades-of-meaning ladder of the year. Students learn how words such as gigantic, immense, and massive differ from each other, and how to name the opposite end (miniature, slender, compact). A second ladder covers room: cramped to spacious. The words repeat dense, tangle, and clumsy from earlier units in new descriptions, and every word can be tested against a picture, which keeps abstract language tied to something visible.

words.def: Extremely large, much bigger than normal.
words.ex: We stared at the gigantic pumpkin that won first prize at the fair.
words.ex2: A gigantic blue whale can be longer than two school buses.
words.nonExample: A single grain of rice is not gigantic.

apps.academic: In science, gigantic animals such as whales are measured in meters, not centimeters.
apps.spoken: That sandwich is gigantic; I can't finish it.
apps.writing: Use gigantic when big is not strong enough to describe something.

cloze2.s: An ___ crowd filled the park, spreading from the fountain to the far gates.

words.ex: Eight strong workers moved the massive stone off the road.
words.ex2: A massive oak tree stood in the middle of the park.
words.nonExample: A feather floating in the air is not massive.

apps.academic: In science, a massive object has a lot of matter and is hard to move.

words.def: Much smaller than the usual size; a tiny copy.
words.ex: Dad built a miniature train that fit on the kitchen table.
words.ex2: The museum had a miniature model of the whole city.
words.nonExample: A full-size school bus is not miniature.

apps.spoken: I love the miniature chairs in my dollhouse.
apps.writing: Use miniature for a very small copy of something real.

cloze.s: The artist painted a ___ portrait that was smaller than a postage stamp.

misuse.s: The miniature elephant was taller than the school and as heavy as a house.

words.def: Thin in a graceful way; long and narrow.
words.ex: The slender birch tree swayed in the breeze.
words.ex2: A slender vase held a single red flower.
words.nonExample: A thick, heavy log is not slender.

apps.spoken: She has slender fingers for playing the piano.
apps.writing: Use slender for something thin that also looks neat or graceful.

cloze2.s: A ___ heron stood on one long leg in the shallow water, still as a statue.

misuse.s: The slender tree trunk was so thick that ten children could not circle it with their arms.
misuse.why: Slender means thin; a trunk that ten children cannot circle is thick.

words.def: Large and heavy in a way that is hard to carry or fit.
words.ex: The bulky winter coat barely fit in the locker.
words.ex2: Carrying the bulky box up the stairs took two people.
words.nonExample: A thin sheet of paper is not bulky.

apps.academic: Bulky items take up a lot of space in a truck or a closet.

apps.writing: Use bulky when the size makes something awkward to carry.

cloze2.s: Nina struggled through the doorway with a ___ package that blocked her view.

apps.academic: A spacious room has enough floor area for many people to move around.
apps.spoken: Our new car is spacious, so everyone has legroom.
apps.writing: Use spacious to describe a room, car, or yard with plenty of room.

cloze2.s: The cat stretched out on the ___ porch and rolled in the sun.

misuse.s: The spacious closet was so tiny that only one shoe fit inside.
misuse.why: Spacious means roomy; a closet with room for one shoe is tiny.

words.def: Too small, with not enough room to move.
words.ex: Six kids squeezed into the cramped back seat of the car.
words.ex2: The cramped elevator felt hot with so many people inside.
words.nonExample: A big open gym with only a few people is not cramped.

apps.academic: A cramped room may be too small for the number of people in it.
apps.spoken: It was cramped on the bus, so I stood.
apps.writing: Use cramped to show that there is not enough room.

cloze2.s: The ___ kitchen had space for only one cook at a time.

misuse.s: The cramped stadium had lots of room, and everyone could stretch out and dance.
misuse.why: Cramped means too little room; a stadium with lots of room is the opposite.

visual.alt: Several children squeezed together in a small car seat.

words.def: Small and neatly packed, using very little room.
words.ex: Her compact car was easy to park in a tiny spot.
words.ex2: The compact tent folded into a bag the size of a loaf of bread.
words.nonExample: A huge, sprawling mansion is not compact.

senses.example: He had to compact the trash to make it fit in the can.

apps.academic: A compact design saves space, which matters when engineers build for small places.
apps.spoken: I like my compact umbrella because it fits in my bag.
apps.writing: Use compact for something small on purpose, so it fits easily.

cloze2.s: Because the apartment is small, they chose a ___ table that folds against the wall.

words.def: Very tall, seeming to rise high above everything near it.

words.ex2: We looked up at the towering redwood trees in the park.
words.nonExample: A small bush near the ground is not towering.

apps.spoken: That is a towering building, and I can't see the top.
apps.writing: Use towering for something so tall that you look up to see it.

misuse.why: Towering means very tall; an ant as tall as a grain of rice is tiny.

passage.title: The Hall of Sizes
paras: Our class visited the Hall of Sizes at the city museum. The room was spacious, with a ceiling as high as a three-story building. In the middle hung a gigantic model of a blue whale. Its massive tail curled right over our heads.

Beside it, a towering statue of a king looked down at us. Its immense hands were each as big as a car. Along the other wall, glass cases held miniature houses, tiny chairs, and a compact toy train no longer than a pencil.
Jada pressed her nose to the glass. "Look at this slender ship," she said. "It is smaller than my hand, but the sails are perfect."
Then our teacher led us into the next room, a cramped hallway. Our bulky winter coats made it even harder to walk through.
On the bus ride back, Jada said her favorite thing was the smallest model. "Big things are exciting," she said, "but tiny things make you look closer."

qs.q: In paragraph 1, the word "massive" describes the whale's tail as
qs.why: The tail curls over the students' heads, so it must be large, and massive adds that it is heavy.

qs.q: Why did the coats make the hallway harder to walk through?
choices: The coats were too thin to keep anyone warm.
The coats took up room in a narrow space.
The coats belonged to the museum.
qs.why: The coats were bulky and the hallway was cramped, so there was not enough room.

qs.q: Which detail shows that the toy train was very small?
choices: It was inside a glass case.
It stood beside a steam engine.
Jada pressed her nose to the glass.
It was no longer than a pencil.
qs.why: Comparing the train to a pencil tells how small it is.

qs.q: Which sentence best tells what Jada learned?
choices: Small things can be interesting because you look at them closely.
Museums should only show tiny models.
A bus is bigger than a whale.
qs.why: Jada says that tiny things make you look closer.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten exact words for size and room, place them on shades-of-meaning ladders, and test each word against a picture. They read a museum narrative that uses all the words and then write descriptions with exact size words.

notes.va.gigantic.adj: Gigantic sits near the top of the size ladder. Ask students to compare it with big and with huge and place the three words on a line.
notes.va.immense.adj: Immense often describes wide spaces, such as oceans and deserts. Contrast it with massive, which feels heavy and solid.
notes.va.massive.adj: Massive adds weight to size. Ask: can something be big but not massive? A big, light balloon is a good example.
notes.va.miniature.adj: Miniature often means a small copy of a real thing, not just anything small. Show a toy car beside a real photograph of a car.
notes.va.slender.adj: Slender is usually positive, while skinny can be negative. Show how slender and bulky sit at opposite ends of a thickness line.
notes.va.bulky.adj: Bulky is about size that gets in the way. Model bulk + -y. Ask students what they carry that is bulky in winter.
notes.va.spacious.adj: Spacious is the room-ladder word at the top. Model space + -ious with the dropped e. Pair it with cramped for opposite pictures.
notes.va.cramped.adj: Cramped is about too little room for the number of people or things. Pair with spacious on the room ladder.
notes.va.compact.adj: Compact is small by design. It is a multiple-meaning word, but the unit teaches the adjective. Show a folding umbrella as a model of compact.
notes.va.towering.adj: Towering is about height, not width. Show tower + -ing. Ask which towering thing students have looked up at.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The story says the statue's hands were each as big as a car. Big does not feel strong enough. Immense says it is huge. I can show a size ladder: big, huge, immense. I choose the word that matches the picture in my head.'

Which size word do you want to use in your own writing this week?
misconceptions: Gigantic, immense, and massive are exactly the same.
Miniature just means any small thing.
extend: Measure three objects in the room and write a sentence for each using an exact size word.
Design a spacious room and a cramped room on paper and label each with the unit words.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit the size ladder two days later and again after a week by putting new objects on it. Reuse dense, tangle, and clumsy in descriptions of the museum pictures.
